DTECH-CTX-G2.title: Lanternfish design notes and retrospective
DTECH-CTX-G2.text:
LANTERNFISH - DESIGN NOTES AND RETROSPECTIVE
Author: Dashiell Marrow, SRE I, Cindervale Systems. Written December 2025 for the SRE team wiki.

Problem
The checkout path (cart-api -> pricing -> payments-gateway) had a p99 of about 1,380 ms against an SLO target of 900 ms. Traces showed unexplained gaps before outbound calls that no span covered. We suspected DNS but had no per-pod data. CoreDNS exposes metrics per CoreDNS replica, only for the queries that reach it, and it sees a client's search-domain expansion as several unrelated queries rather than one slow lookup.

Design
Lanternfish is a Rust sidecar built on the tokio async runtime, using the hickory-proto crate to parse DNS messages. It is injected into pods on the checkout path.
- The pod uses dnsPolicy None with a dnsConfig whose first nameserver is 127.0.0.1. Lanternfish listens on 127.0.0.1:53 over UDP; only the sidecar container gets the NET_BIND_SERVICE capability.
- Each query is forwarded unchanged to the cluster DNS service IP. Lanternfish times the lookup from the moment the query arrives from the application to the moment the response is written back.
- It exports a Prometheus histogram, lanternfish_lookup_seconds, with 12 buckets from 1 ms to 2.5 s and the labels qtype, rcode and upstream. The queried name is deliberately NOT a label, to keep cardinality bounded.
- A counter, lanternfish_search_expansions_total, counts queries for names that end in one of the pod's search suffixes and come back NXDOMAIN.
- The existing Prometheus scrapes it every 15 seconds; no new storage was needed.
- The second nameserver line in dnsConfig points straight at the cluster DNS IP, with options timeout:1, so a crashed sidecar costs a one-second retry rather than an outage.

Why a sidecar
We considered three options:
1. CoreDNS metrics. Already existed, but aggregated per replica rather than per pod, and blind to how many expansions one application lookup triggered.
2. An eBPF probe on each node. Per-pod data without touching pods, but our GKE nodes ran Container-Optimized OS, nobody on the team had written eBPF before, and we estimated 4 to 6 weeks.
3. A sidecar. Per pod by construction, easy to remove, and about 2 weeks of work.
We chose the sidecar. The trade-off: it only sees pods it is injected into, and it adds one local hop to every lookup.

Rollout
Lanternfish ran on the 14 deployments of the checkout path for three weeks.

Findings
- 31% of p99 latency on the checkout path came from DNS resolution.
- The main cause was the default ndots:5. External names such as the payment processor's API have fewer than five dots, so the resolver tried every search domain first. On GKE that meant up to 10 failed queries (A and AAAA for each of 5 search domains) before the real lookup.
- A smaller share came from occasional 5-second stalls caused by a known conntrack race when A and AAAA queries go out in parallel over UDP.

Fix
- Priya Oduya (senior SRE) reviewed the design and ran the rollout of the fix; I wrote the sidecar, the dashboards and the analysis.
- Checkout-path pods moved to ndots:2, and the three external payment endpoints were changed to fully qualified names with a trailing dot.
- NodeLocal DNSCache was enabled on the cluster, which also removed the conntrack stalls.
- Checkout p99 fell from 1,380 ms to 910 ms, and DNS dropped to about 6% of p99.

Overhead and limitations
- Median added latency is about 0.3 ms per lookup; each sidecar uses about 6 MiB of memory and under 5 millicores of CPU.
- UDP only: queries that fall back to TCP after a truncated response are passed through and not measured.
- After the fix we removed the sidecar from 9 of the 14 deployments and kept it on 5 as a canary.
- It was never deployed to the other two clusters, and it has not been open-sourced.

DTECH-CTX-C1.title: Quarrystone take-home candidate FAQ
DTECH-CTX-C1.text:
QUARRYSTONE TAKE-HOME - CANDIDATE FAQ
Forwarded by Pilar Okonkwo-Reyes, Technical Recruiter. Compiled from questions earlier candidates asked about the Pager Quiet Windows exercise. Different interviewers wrote different answers.

Q: How long should I spend on it?
A: Please keep it under 3 hours. We are not grading polish.

Q: How big are the inputs?
A: Each host has at most 200,000 windows, so an O(n log n) sort-based solution is what we expect.

Q: Do windows that touch, like [5, 10] and [10, 12], merge when grace is 0?
A: No. Ends are exclusive, so [5, 10] and [10, 12] stay separate unless grace is at least 1.

Q: What languages can I use?
A: Python 3.10+ or Go 1.22+, standard library only.

Q: Can I use sortedcontainers or another package for part 2?
A: Yes, any package on PyPI is fine as long as you pin it in requirements.txt.

Q: What does the grader check first?
A: The edge cases. Touching windows always merge, even with grace 0, and zero-length windows are dropped. Most failed submissions get one of those wrong.

Q: What is the performance bar?
A: The hidden cases go up to 2 million windows per host, and the reference solution finishes in under 1 second in Python. If yours takes a few seconds that is fine; we cut off at 5 seconds.

Q: When is it due?
A: You have 48 hours from when the link opens. Most people spend a full day on it.

Q: Should part 2 count grace gaps as quiet time?
A: No, only minutes actually inside a window count.

DTECH-CTX-G1.title: Quarrystone take-home: Pager Quiet Windows (problem statement)
DTECH-CTX-G1.text:
QUARRYSTONE ANALYTICS - PLATFORM TEAM TAKE-HOME (v3)
Problem: Pager Quiet Windows

Background
Our on-call tool lets engineers schedule "quiet windows" during which non-critical pages for a host are held back. Engineers create windows independently, so the list for one host arrives unsorted and often overlapping. Before we push windows to the pager we collapse them into the smallest equivalent list.

Part 1: merge_windows(windows, grace)
Input:
- windows: a list of pairs [start, end], in integer minutes since the start of the quarter. A window covers minute start (inclusive) up to end (exclusive), so [10, 20] covers 10 minutes.
- grace: an integer number of minutes.

Rules:
1. If any window has end < start, raise ValueError with the message "inverted window at index i", where i is the index of the FIRST such window in the input list as given (before any sorting).
2. A window with end == start covers no time and is dropped silently. A dropped window must not bridge two other windows.
3. After sorting by start, a window merges into the current merged window when its start <= current end + grace. Windows that touch (next start == current end) therefore always merge, even with grace 0.
4. Grace only decides whether two windows merge; it never extends a window. A merged window ends at the largest end among the windows it absorbed.
5. Return the merged windows sorted by start, as a new list of [start, end] pairs. Do not mutate the input list or the pairs inside it.

Examples
Example 1: windows = [[10, 20], [15, 30], [40, 50]], grace = 0
Output: [[10, 30], [40, 50]]

Example 2: windows = [[5, 10], [10, 12], [13, 20]], grace = 0
Output: [[5, 12], [13, 20]]
([5, 10] and [10, 12] touch, so they merge. The gap from 12 to 13 is 1 minute, which is larger than grace 0.)

Example 3: windows = [[5, 10], [10, 12], [13, 20]], grace = 1
Output: [[5, 20]]
(Note the result is [5, 20], not [5, 21]: grace never extends a window.)

Example 4: windows = [[30, 30], [1, 4], [2, 3]], grace = 5
Output: [[1, 4]]
([30, 30] is dropped; [2, 3] lies inside [1, 4].)

Example 5: windows = [[0, 10], [11, 11], [12, 20]], grace = 1
Output: [[0, 10], [12, 20]]
([11, 11] is dropped before merging, so it cannot bridge the gap between 10 and 12.)

Example 6: windows = [[7, 3], [1, 2], [9, 4]], grace = 0
Raises ValueError("inverted window at index 0")

Example 7: windows = [], grace = 10
Output: []

Part 2: total_quiet_minutes(windows, grace)
Return the total number of minutes covered by the output of merge_windows. A gap that grace bridged is counted, because the merged window spans it. For Example 1 the answer is 30, for Example 3 it is 15, and for Example 7 it is 0.

Constraints
- 0 <= len(windows) <= 200,000
- 0 <= start, end <= 10^9
- 0 <= grace <= 60
- Your solution must run in O(n log n) time. Our reference solution runs in under 1 second in Python for n = 200,000.
- Python 3.10+ or Go 1.22+. Standard library only.

What we look at
Correctness on our hidden cases (including every edge case above), readability, the tests you write yourself, and a short note (under 200 words) explaining your approach and its complexity. Please do not spend more than 3 hours.

Live follow-up
In the follow-up interview we will ask how your design changes if windows arrive one at a time from a stream and the pager needs to ask "is minute t quiet?" at any moment.

items.question: Let's do a small API design. A URL shortener: what endpoints would you have, what does each one return, and what should happen if two people shorten the exact same long URL?
items.answer:
I'd keep it to three endpoints. A POST to /shorten takes the long URL and returns the short code, the short URL, and a 201. A GET on /{code} returns a 301 or 302 redirect to the original, and a 404 if the code doesn't exist. Optionally a GET on /{code}/stats returns the click count and creation time.

For the duplicate case, I'd make shortening idempotent: hash the long URL, look it up, and if a code already exists, return that same code with a 200 instead of creating a second one. That keeps the mapping one-to-one and avoids wasting codes. If someone wants a distinct code per user, that's a different product decision, and I'd handle it by scoping the lookup to the account.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Let's trace one. Lower bound binary search: lo is zero, hi is the length, while lo is less than hi, mid is lo plus hi over two, if a of mid is less than target then lo is mid plus one, otherwise hi is mid. Walk me through it on one, two, two, two, five with target two. Tell me lo, hi and mid at every step.
items.answer:
Array is [1, 2, 2, 2, 5], target 2, n = 5, so lo = 0, hi = 5.

Step 1: lo = 0, hi = 5, mid = 2. a[2] = 2, not less than 2, so hi = 2.
Step 2: lo = 0, hi = 2, mid = 1. a[1] = 2, not less than 2, so hi = 1.
Step 3: lo = 0, hi = 1, mid = 0. a[0] = 1, which is less than 2, so lo = 1.
Now lo = 1 and hi = 1, so the loop ends and we return lo = 1, the first index where the value is 2.

items.question: Which isolation level?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): Before we start, have you ever built a double-entry ledger? Either way, design one for grower payouts: the tables, how a payout moves money between accounts, and how you guarantee a retried payout never pays twice.

NATIVELY: I haven't built a production double-entry ledger, but I've worked on idempotent, event-driven payment flows, so let me design one.

Tables: accounts (id, owner_type, currency), journal_entries (id, idempotency_key unique, created_at), and postings (entry_id, account_id, amount, signed). Every entry's postings sum to zero.

A payout: debit the grower-payable account, credit the grower's cash account, in one transaction. Escrow holds sit in a separate liability account until settlement releases them.

For no double pay: the idempotency key on the entry is unique, so a retry hits the constraint and returns the original entry instead of posting again. The bank transfer itself carries the same key, so the provider dedupes too.
items.answer: For a payout posting, **read committed** is enough. The entry and its postings go in one transaction, and the unique idempotency key is what actually prevents a double pay, not the isolation level. I'd only go to **repeatable read** if a payout reads multiple balances and needs a consistent snapshot across them.

items.question: interviewer wants approach only: detect a cycle in a linked list and find the node where it starts. no code, 3 sentences max
items.answer: Use Floyd's tortoise and hare: move one pointer one step and the other two steps until they meet, which proves a cycle exists. Then reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time; the node where they meet again is the start of the cycle. It's O(n) time and O(1) space.

items.question: Okay, can you beat n log k? Say the array is huge and k is close to the number of distinct values.
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): Given an array of integers and a number k, return the k most frequent elements. For example one, one, one, two, two, three with k equal to two gives you one and two. How would you solve it?

NATIVELY: ## Approach
Count frequencies with a hash map, then keep the top k. Two clean options: bucket sort by frequency for O(n) time, or a min-heap of size k for O(n log k). I'll use the heap since it's simple and doesn't depend on frequency bounds.

## Code
```python
import heapq
from collections import Counter

def topKFrequent(nums, k):
    counts = Counter(nums)
    return heapq.nlargest(k, counts.keys(), key=counts.get)
```

## Complexity
Time O(n log k), since we count in O(n) and pull the k largest from the map. Space O(n) for the frequency map.
INTERVIEWER (heard): Why a heap?

NATIVELY: Because I only need the top k, not a full ordering. A min-heap of size k keeps the k largest frequencies seen so far, and each new element either gets rejected against the smallest or replaces it, so every push and pop is O(log k) instead of O(log n). That's the win when k is much smaller than the number of distinct elements. If k were close to n, or I needed everything sorted, I'd just sort the counts instead.
items.answer: Yes, when k is close to the number of distinct values, the heap loses its edge, so I'd bucket sort by frequency instead. Frequencies are bounded by n, so I build an array of buckets indexed by count and read off the top k. That's O(n) time and O(n) space, no log factor at all.

items.question: Most of our control plane tooling is in Go. Walk me through how goroutines get scheduled onto OS threads, when you'd reach for a channel versus a mutex, and tell me honestly how much Go you've written in production.
items.answer:
Goroutines are multiplexed onto OS threads by the Go runtime scheduler, which uses an M:N model. Each goroutine starts on a small stack, and the scheduler maps many goroutines onto a pool of OS threads. There's a GMP model: G is the goroutine, M is the OS thread, and P is a logical processor that holds a run queue. Each P has a local run queue, and there's a global queue too. When a goroutine blocks on a syscall, the M detaches from the P so another M can pick up the P and keep running other goroutines. Blocking on a channel or mutex parks the goroutine and frees the P to run something else. The scheduler also does work-stealing: an idle P steals goroutines from other Ps' run queues. Preemption happens at safe points, and since Go 1.14 there's asynchronous preemption so a tight loop can't starve others.

For channels versus mutexes: I reach for a channel when I'm passing ownership of data or coordinating goroutines, like a pipeline or a worker pool where one goroutine hands work to another. I reach for a mutex when I'm protecting shared state that multiple goroutines read and write, like a map or a counter, where the point is mutual exclusion rather than communication. The common guidance is channels for orchestration and mutexes for state, and I try not to force one where the other fits better.

On production Go: I want to be straight with you. My Go has mostly been in side projects and coursework rather than a production control plane. My homelab is a 4-node Raspberry Pi k3s cluster managed through Flux GitOps, hosting a self-hosted Matrix server, with Loki and Grafana for logs. That's where I've done most of my Go. I haven't shipped Go in a production control plane at the scale you're describing, so I'd be ramping up on your codebase, though the concurrency model and the systems thinking carry over.

items.question: Tell me about Project Tern. Why split settlement into three services instead of keeping one, and how did you cut over without paying a carrier twice?
items.answer:
I led Project Tern, a rewrite of our carrier-settlement service from a Rails monolith into three Go services, with a working group of 4 engineers and 1 QA analyst over 7 months. We split it because settlement has distinct concerns: quoting rates, processing shipment events, and reconciling invoices against booked loads. Keeping them in one monolith meant a slow rate-quote path and a nightly reconciliation job that couldn't scale independently. The reconciliation job compares carrier invoices against booked loads, and it cut monthly mismatches from 312 to 41, so that separation paid off.

On the cutover, I don't have the exact mechanism in front of me. What I'd confirm is how we sequenced the switch so a carrier wasn't paid twice, and I can walk through that once I check the runbook.

items.question: Why a heap?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): Given an array of integers and a number k, return the k most frequent elements. For example one, one, one, two, two, three with k equal to two gives you one and two. How would you solve it?

NATIVELY: ## Approach
Count frequencies with a hash map, then keep the top k. Two clean options: bucket sort by frequency for O(n) time, or a min-heap of size k for O(n log k). I'll use the heap since it's simple and doesn't depend on frequency bounds.

## Code
```python
import heapq
from collections import Counter

def topKFrequent(nums, k):
    counts = Counter(nums)
    return heapq.nlargest(k, counts.keys(), key=counts.get)
```

## Complexity
Time O(n log k), since we count in O(n) and pull the k largest from the map. Space O(n) for the frequency map.
items.answer: Because I only need the top k, not a full ordering. A min-heap of size k keeps the k largest frequencies seen so far, and each new element either gets rejected against the smallest or replaces it, so every push and pop is O(log k) instead of O(log n). That's the win when k is much smaller than the number of distinct elements. If k were close to n, or I needed everything sorted, I'd just sort the counts instead.

items.question: Now say windows arrive one at a time from a stream, and the pager can ask is minute t quiet at any moment. What changes in your design?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): Okay, let's go over your take-home. For example two and example three, walk me through what your merge returns and why the two outputs are different.

NATIVELY: I don't have the actual outputs for examples two and three in front of me, so let me walk through the logic and what each should return.

Both examples go through the same merge: sort the windows by start, then sweep through and merge any window that overlaps or is within grace of the current one. The difference in output comes down to whether the gap between two windows is small enough for grace to bridge it. If the gap is at or under grace, the two collapse into one window spanning both. If it's larger, they stay separate.

Can you pull up the two examples so I can point at the exact numbers?
INTERVIEWER (heard): And the complexity?

NATIVELY: Sorting dominates, so it's **O(n log n)** time. The sweep after that is a single pass, so it's linear, and the merged output is at most n windows, so **O(n)** space. That matches the constraint in the prompt, and it's why the reference solution stays under a second at n = 200,000.
items.answer: The batch merge goes away. I'd keep the merged windows in a structure ordered by start, and on each new window, merge it into the tail if it overlaps or is within grace, otherwise append. For "is minute t quiet," I need to know whether t falls inside any merged window, so a binary search over the sorted starts gives O(log n) per query, and each arrival is O(log n) amortized.

items.question: Have you run Postgres in production? Say there's a table with a couple billion event rows and vacuum takes hours. Would you partition it, how, and what gets harder once you do?
items.answer:
I've run Postgres, though not at that scale, so I'd reason from first principles. A couple billion rows with hours-long vacuums, yes, I'd partition, almost certainly by range on time, monthly or weekly, so autovacuum works per-partition and old data drops by detaching instead of deleting.

What gets harder: cross-partition queries and unique constraints need the partition key, and I have to manage partition creation and pruning so you don't end up with thousands of them.

items.question: Why a sidecar?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): Your resume says Lanternfish showed 41 percent of p99 on checkout was DNS. How did you actually measure that, and what was Lanternfish doing under the hood?

NATIVELY: The resume says 31 percent, not 41, so I'd correct that first. Lanternfish is a Rust sidecar that exports per-pod DNS lookup latency to Prometheus, so we could see DNS time broken out per pod instead of buried in total request latency. That's what showed 31 percent of p99 on the checkout path was DNS resolution.
items.answer: We looked at three options. CoreDNS metrics were already there, but they're aggregated per replica, not per pod, and blind to how many expansions one lookup triggered. An eBPF probe would've given per-pod data without touching pods, but our nodes ran Container-Optimized OS, nobody on the team had written eBPF, and we estimated 4 to 6 weeks. A sidecar is per pod by construction, easy to remove, and about 2 weeks of work. The trade-off is it only sees pods it's injected into, and it adds one local hop per lookup.
